With all the news of hacking team lately, I though people might be interested in learning about a high security Linux system, Qubes OS

Qubes does provide windows integration tools, allowing you to use a windows 7 install seamlessly. Windows 8 support is forthcoming. The only major complaint I have with Qubes is the lack of graphics acceleration, as there is no means to virtualize graphics acceleration, and there may never be a secure way to virtualize graphics acceleration.

Also, my very first submission anywhere! (please be gentle)

Is this like CoreOS? It seems, in principle, it's similar to virtualization used by smart phone operating systems like Android. I think this is an interesting take on securing a desktop from applications. I also think Ubuntu Core and Snappy is an interesting take as well.

(I'd give you an upvoat but hit my quota, I'm 4 ccp shy of upvoat impunity)

I feel like running everything inside a virtual machine would be way too slow for practical use. Sandbox's seem like a much more practical option, from what I've heard. Although, I guess you can't really get more secure than a virtual machine.

I've been using my Thinkpad X230 tablet to run Qubes, and the main slowdown comes from the hard drive, but with SSDs becoming more and more commonplace, that will be less of an issue. The only other major (easily solvable) technical issue is ram. 4 GB of ram is not really enough, 8, 12, or 16 would be much better.

On sandboxing, look up sandbox breakout attacks and permissions elevation. Both of these are, unfortunately fairly common bugs. To do the same thing to Qubes, you have to get a Xen breakout. Only one Xen breakout has ever been identified (never used in a attack), and it was by the Qubes team themselves.

Qubes might be overkill for most people, especially certain features like anti-evil maid, but I enjoy the increased security. It is worth noting that Qubes is still very young, likened to a manual transmission sports car. The dev team wants Qubes to become as easy to use as an automatic.
